newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan gives best economic assessment in five years.
newsitem.headline: Japan gives best economic assessment in five years.

text.p: In the government's strongest official assessment of the economy in the last five years, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said on Friday that Japan's economy is on the verge of a self-sustaining recovery.
The EPA said in its annual report, "the present state of the economy is close to one where we can say it is recovering autonomously led by private sector demand."

The report said that, although the pitch of the recovery had slowed after the national sales tax was raised to five percent from three percent in April, the recovery was not threatened and was set to continue.

After years of recession brought on by the bursting of the land and asset price "bubble" of the late 1980s, the economy has spent the most part of the past two years weaning itself away from policy-induced pick-me-ups and has been, in the words of the EPA's monthly reports, gradually recovering.
Betting the economy would begin to run under its own steam and with its pockets now empty, the government has embarked on a policy of fiscal tightening, including April's sales tax rise.
Key to the report was the EPA's argument that virtuous business cycles have begun to form.
Starting from the middle of last year, inventory adjustments at Japanese firms led to a pick-up in production across broad sections of industry, which in turn helped improve employment conditions.
In addition, a weakening of the yen, which makes Japanese products cheaper to customers abroad, led to a boom in exports.
"A relatively solid recovery is continuing," Akira Furukawa, the director of the EPA's national economic research bureau, told Reuters Financial Television.
The EPA has been wrong before, however, prematurely stating that a recovery was underway only to see the economy stall and sputter along.

While stressing it did not want to comment on whether or when Japan's interest rates should be raised, the EPA also said in the report that two years had passed since interest rates were cut to rock bottom levels and firms and individuals should be aware of the risk that interest rates may rise.
The report also said the nation's economy has put the worst of the hangover from the bubble years behind it.

While firms in industry and finance may still have balance sheet problems, these problems had slipped from a macro-economic level to a micro-economic level, losing their potential to hinder growth, the report said.
Looking forward, it said that the key question was now whether the recovery would lead to economic development in the medium to long term.
It said that, although the future remained unclear, the economy now had the will and stamina to embark on drastic reforms and should seize the chance to create free and transparent markets.
In particular, it pointed to the distribution and service sectors as stifling business opportunities through over-regulation and antiquated business practices.
